A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same FINOLA/one-way-wave reconstruction framework, with matching equations and retained ImageNet results despite retitling and substantial expansion. Their main text, figures, tables, equations, and appendices support reliable comparison.

before.justification: v1 Section 3 and Appendix B report original ImageNet reconstruction results, including PSNR measurements and experiments varying channels, paths, resolutions, wave speeds, and initial positions.

after.justification: v2 reports original reconstruction, compression, representation-learning, classification, detection, and segmentation results in Sections 4–5 and Appendices A–C.

M1.justification: The reconstruction framework is retained, but v2 introduces Masked FINOLA with cropped-block inputs and loss computed only on masked pixels. Its element-wise variant compresses the visible block, while its block-wise variant preserves uncompressed features and predicts assigned masked positions, with different decoder architectures (Appendix B.1). These are substantive procedural extensions.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates ImageNet image reconstruction. v2 retains that task and adds quantized image compression on ImageNet and Kodak, masked prediction and ImageNet classification, and COCO object detection and instance segmentation (Sections 4–5, Appendix B). These substantially broaden both datasets and task requirements.

E2.justification: v1 mainly compares against single-path FINOLA and repetition; its DCT/wavelet comparison is conceptual. v2 adds quantitative comparisons with DCT, DWT/DTCWT, convolutional autoencoders, JPEG, and generative-model autoencoders (Tables 5–8 and 15). New downstream comparisons include MAE, SimMIM, MoCo variants, and DETR-based detectors.

E3.justification: v2 extends reconstruction feature resolutions from 16–128 to 8–256 and the path sweep to 16 paths. The all-one-wave comparison changes its repetition control from dimension 3072 to 4096. New protocols include bitrate evaluation, 1600-epoch masked pretraining, linear/transformer probing, and frozen versus fine-tuned COCO backbones. The original 100-epoch reconstruction schedule remains, while the 512×512 image-size experiment disappears.

E4.justification: v2 adds normalization/nonlinearity controls, encoder-size and single-vector-position ablations, embedding sampling/interpolation/PCA, masked-decoder-depth and training-duration studies, and feature-curvature analysis. Existing path-count and wave-speed analyses remain. The detailed four-path spatial-offset sweep in v1 Table 3(b) is omitted, although scattering comparisons are retained and expanded.

E5.justification: v2 Figure 21 introduces box-and-whisker summaries of feature curvature, adding distributional spread reporting absent from v1. Neither version reports benchmark seed counts, repeated-run uncertainty, or confidence intervals. The new plot does not specify its box/whisker conventions, so it should not be interpreted as confidence intervals across training runs.

E6.justification: The original C=2048, M=8 reconstruction PSNR of 28.0 is retained. v2 newly reports 29.1 for M=16 and 30.0 with scattered initial positions, representing added configurations rather than same-setting improvements. It also adds substantial compression and downstream results, including 83.9 ImageNet top-1 accuracy and 49.0 COCO detection AP (Tables 9 and 28). v1's 512×512 reconstruction result of 25.1 is omitted.

T1.justification: v2 corrects the transformed normalization: the denominator's quadratic-form matrix changes from CI - V^-1 J V in v1 Equation 7 to V^T(CI - J)V in v2 Equation 7. Appendix D.1 supplies a stepwise derivation absent from v1. This is a localized mathematical correction; the central diagonalization, superposition argument, and special wave-speed cases remain.

C1.justification: The shared-wave invariance claim remains. However, v2 broadens the introduction and conclusion beyond hidden-wave reconstruction to claim advantages over conventional reconstruction techniques and effective self-supervised learning with lightweight networks. FINOLA and its representation-learning application become central contributions rather than the paper focusing on two extensions of earlier FINOLA.

C2.justification: v2 interprets reconstruction quality through total latent size MC, discusses the tradeoff between texture reconstruction and semantic representation under masking, and connects feature curvature to semantics. It also clarifies that wave speeds are obtained through post-training diagonalization and that diagonalizability is not guaranteed. These substantially extend v1's interpretation of path counts, wave speeds, and spatial shifts.

D1.justification: Beyond v1's architecture and reconstruction-training tables, v2 newly documents attentional pooling, the L2 objective, parallel autoregression, expanded encoder/decoder specifications, and masked-learning/probing/fine-tuning settings. Appendix A.2.3 adds training and inference hardware and timing, including eight V100 GPUs and an Apple M2 CPU. These disclosures substantially improve implementation guidance without establishing changes to every retained experiment.

R1.justification: v1 explicitly builds on Chen et al. (2023), 'Image is first-order norm+linear autoregressive.' v2 removes that citation and presents FINOLA directly. Its positioning also expands substantially into autoregressive language models, contrastive learning, and masked image modeling, including explicit distinctions from MAE's masking and prediction mechanisms.

P1.justification: v2 retitles the paper and extensively rewrites the abstract, introduction, method exposition, and conclusion. It reorganizes the narrative around FINOLA before wave-equation generalization, moves special-speed and scattering discussions into Appendix A, and adds dedicated self-supervised-learning and limitations sections. The appendices are substantially reorganized.

P2.justification: v2 redraws framework diagrams, adds single-path, parallel-execution, and masking illustrations, and removes v1's wave-quartet diagram. The reconstruction plot gains a 16-path column and latent-size contours. Existing reconstruction galleries are relocated or relabeled, while numerous comparison tables, embedding visualizations, training curves, and curvature plots are added.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens evidence and reproducibility: v1's conceptual transform comparison becomes quantitative, new component controls test the FINOLA design, implementation details become more complete, and Appendix D.1 corrects and derives the normalization. These gains exceed mere expansion of scope. Tradeoffs include loss of the detailed spatial-offset sweep and earlier FINOLA attribution, plus a new 27.8 versus 27.7 inconsistency for C=1024, M=16 in Figure 5 and Table 18. Those weaknesses do not outweigh the stronger validation and mathematical documentation.
